\chapter{One, the Other, and the Price}
\label{ch:ta-one-the-other-and-the-price}
\hlchaptermodality{80}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can tell two things apart, choose between them, and ask what one costs.}

Complete TA-C80-price and run the whole counter exchange, from choosing to asking.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[maṟṟadu]{\ta{மற்றது} (maṟṟadu) — the other one}

\label{lesson:TA-C80-other}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{எப்போது}}. Then say: when you come, tell me.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மற்றது}}
\textbf{\ta{மற்றது}} (\emph{maṟṟadu}) — \textquotedblleft{}the other one\textquotedblright{}.

\ta{இது} and \ta{அது} name a thing by where it stands: near me, over there. \ta{மற்றது} names it by what it is not — the one that is \emph{left}, once you have picked one up.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{இது} \ta{வேண்டும்}. \ta{மற்றது} \ta{வேண்டாம்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{idu vēṇḍum. maṟṟadu vēṇḍām.} — \textquotedblleft{}I want this one. Not the other.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The tail of the word is \textbf{\ta{அது}}, the same \emph{that one} that ends \ta{அதனால்}. Tamil builds a surprising amount out of that small word, and once you hear it inside a longer one you can usually guess what the longer one is doing.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A third way to point at a thing, once two of them are on the table.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{maṟṟadu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{idu vēṇḍum. maṟṟadu vēṇḍām.}
  \item \emph{Notice:} the \ta{அது} at the end of \ta{மற்றது} and at the start of \ta{அதனால்}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{எப்போது}}, then say \emph{varum pōdu}, then say \emph{maṟṟadu}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{ām / illai}, read \textbf{\ta{குடி}} and say \emph{-kkāga} — three distances back — then set two of them against each other, one and the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\ta{இது} names a thing by where it is. What does \ta{மற்றது} name it by? (\textbf{By being the one left over.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[oṉṟu … maṟṟadu]{\ta{ஒன்று} … \ta{மற்றது} — one here, the other there}

\label{lesson:TA-C80-one-and-other}



\begin{quote}
Say: when you come, tell me. Then say \emph{the other one}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: a pair, split across two halves}]
\textbf{\ta{ஒன்று}} has been the number \emph{one} since chapter seven. Put \textbf{\ta{மற்றது}} opposite it and the number stops counting and starts distributing.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{ஒன்று} \ta{இங்கே}, \ta{மற்றது} \ta{அங்கே}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{oṉṟu iṅgē, maṟṟadu aṅgē.} — \textquotedblleft{}One is here, the other is there.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Two halves, no joining word between them, and no verb in either. Tamil sets them side by side and the pairing does the work — the same silence you first met in \textbf{\ta{இவர்} \ta{என்} \ta{நண்பர்}}.

It works with any two facts you can already state:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{ஒன்று} \ta{பெரிய} \ta{வீடு}, \ta{மற்றது} \ta{சிறிய} \ta{வீடு}.}
\end{quote}

Chapter seventy-four joined two things into one list. This does the opposite: it takes two things and holds them apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both directions now: a way to put two things together, and a way to tell them apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{oṉṟu iṅgē, maṟṟadu aṅgē}
  \item \emph{Build:} \emph{oṉṟu periya vīḍu, maṟṟadu siṟiya vīḍu}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{pālum tēnīrum} against \emph{oṉṟu … maṟṟadu} — held together, then held apart
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{varum pōdu}, then say \emph{maṟṟadu}, then say the whole pair
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{niṟuttu}, read \textbf{\ta{சரியா}} and say \emph{eppōdu} — three distances back — then set two of them against each other, one and the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many joining words stand between the two halves? (\textbf{None — the pair itself is the join.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maṟṟadu]{\ta{மற்றது} — a doubling you have read twice before}

\label{lesson:TA-W35-read-marradu}



\begin{quote}
Before the page: say \emph{one here, the other there}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{மற்றது} — \ta{ற} standing on \ta{ற}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{ம}} & \emph{ma} & the letter on its own \\
\textbf{\ta{ற்}} & \emph{ṟ} & \ta{ற} with a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}} \\
\textbf{\ta{ற}} & \emph{ṟa} & \ta{ற} again, this time carrying its vowel \\
\textbf{\ta{து}} & \emph{du} & \ta{த} with the \textbf{\ta{ு}} sign \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{ம} · \ta{ற்} · \ta{ற} · \ta{து} $\to$ \ta{மற்றது}}
\end{quote}

The middle is the doubling you read in \textbf{\ta{சட்டை}} with \ta{ட} and in \textbf{\ta{எப்போது}} with \ta{ப}. A third letter, the same shape of seam: one wearing a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}}, leaning on its twin.

Once you have seen it three times it stops being a thing to work out. It is a shape.

The last two letters spell \textbf{\ta{து}}, and the word they close is \textbf{\ta{அது}} — the \emph{that one} the lesson before pointed out. On the page you can see the whole word being built out of things you have.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{ம}} — then \textbf{\ta{ற்}} — then \textbf{\ta{ற}} — then \textbf{\ta{து}}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{மற்றது}}, then \textbf{\ta{எப்போது}}, then \textbf{\ta{சட்டை}} — three doublings, three letters
  \item \emph{Point to:} in each one, the letter carrying the \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{maṟṟadu}, then say \emph{oṉṟu iṅgē, maṟṟadu aṅgē}, then read \textbf{\ta{மற்றது}}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{tiṟa}, \emph{nāṉ uḷḷē varalāmā?} and \emph{appōdu} — three distances back — then set two of them against each other, one and the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{மற்றது}}. Which letter is written twice? (\textbf{\ta{ற} — the first one with a \ta{புள்ளி}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vilai evvaḷavu?]{\ta{விலை} \ta{எவ்வளவு}? — how much does it cost?}

\label{lesson:TA-C80-price}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{மற்றது}}. Then say: one here, the other there.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the question the shop is for}
\textbf{\ta{விலை} \ta{எவ்வளவு}?} (\emph{vilai evvaḷavu?}) — \textquotedblleft{}How much does it cost?\textquotedblright{}

Both words have been yours for a long time. \textbf{\ta{எவ்வளவு}} came in chapter thirty-nine and \textbf{\ta{விலை}} in chapter sixty-eight. Standing side by side they are the question a shop exists for, and until now nothing put them side by side.

No verb, and no word for \emph{is}. Tamil names the thing and asks about it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{விலை} \ta{எவ்வளவு}?} — the price, how much?
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{இது} \ta{எவ்வளவு}?} — this one, how much?
\end{quote}

Then chapter seventy-five lets you check what you heard, or push back on it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{விலை} \ta{குறைவா}?} — \emph{vilai kuṟaivā?} — \textquotedblleft{}Is the price low?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ta{குறைவு}} is the shortfall word from chapter fifty-six, and the \textbf{-\ta{ஆ}} on the end is the question ending. Two chapters, one sentence you can say across a counter.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A whole shop exchange: choose one of two, ask the price, question the answer.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Ask:} \emph{vilai evvaḷavu?}
  \item \emph{Ask:} \emph{idu evvaḷavu?}
  \item \emph{Push back:} \emph{vilai kuṟaivā?}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{oṉṟu iṅgē, maṟṟadu aṅgē}, then read \textbf{\ta{மற்றது}}, then ask the price
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{mūḍu}, say \emph{āṉāl} and read \textbf{\ta{எப்போது}} — three distances back — then set two of them against each other, one and the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many words does it take to ask a price in Tamil, and how many verbs? (\textbf{Two words, and no verb.})
\end{tcolorbox}
